title: Criminal Defense Lawyer Cost: Flat Fees, Retainers, Public Defenders (2026)
description: What a criminal defense lawyer costs for misdemeanors and felonies, flat vs hourly fees, public defender eligibility, and why bail is not a legal fee.
h1: How much does a criminal defense lawyer cost?
summary: Criminal defense lawyers charge a flat fee for misdemeanors and routine cases or bill hourly against a retainer for serious felonies; contingency fees are prohibited. Clio's 2025 average in its criminal category is $216 per hour, against $349 for all lawyers. If jail is possible and you cannot afford a lawyer, you are entitled to appointed counsel; eligibility tests vary, and Florida, for example, uses 200% of the federal poverty guidelines and a $50 application fee.
body:
First question: do you qualify for a public defender?

If you cannot afford a lawyer, you have a constitutional right to one in many criminal cases. The Supreme Court held in 1963 that states must provide counsel to indigent defendants facing felony charges [1], and in 1972 extended that to any case, misdemeanor included, that results in imprisonment [2]. So if jail is a possible outcome, ask for appointed counsel at your first court appearance.

How eligibility is decided

Each state sets its own test. Florida is a clear example: the clerk finds you indigent if your income is at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines for your household, or if you receive TANF cash assistance, poverty-related veterans' benefits or SSI; owning $2,500 or more in property or equity (excluding your home and one car worth up to $5,000) creates a presumption that you are not indigent [3].

Example (Florida test, 2026 guidelines): the 2026 poverty guideline is $15,960 for one person and $33,000 for a family of four [4]. At 200%: 2 × $15,960 = $31,920 for one person; 2 × $33,000 = $66,000 for a family of four.

"Free" counsel is not always free. Florida charges a $50 application fee for court-appointed counsel, payable within 7 days, but a person found indigent cannot be refused a lawyer for failing to pay it; unpaid amounts can be assessed at the end of the case [3]. Many states also charge fees or seek reimbursement for appointed counsel after the case. Ask the public defender's office how it works in your county.

How private defense lawyers charge

If you hire a lawyer, expect one of two structures:

  • Flat fee. Common for misdemeanors and routine felonies. One fee covers a defined stage, typically through a plea or dismissal. Trial is often a separate, larger fee.
  • Hourly against a retainer. Common for serious felonies, cases with many hearings or uncertain scope. The retainer is held in a client trust account and drawn down as the lawyer works [7].

No contingency fees: ABA Model Rule 1.5(d)(2) prohibits a contingent fee for representing a criminal defendant [6]. A lawyer who offers to be paid "only if you win" is breaking the rules most states follow.

Clio's 2025 data puts the average hourly rate in its "criminal" category at $216, well below the $349 average for all lawyers [5]. Experienced private defense lawyers often charge more than that average, so treat it as a reference point, not a price.

Misdemeanor vs felony: where the hours go

What usually drives lawyer time
StageMisdemeanorFelony
Arraignment and bailUsually one short hearingMay include a contested bail or detention hearing
Evidence reviewPolice report, maybe videoLab reports, phone extractions, multiple witnesses
MotionsOccasionalSuppression and other motions are common
Preliminary hearing or grand juryRareCommon, depending on the state
TrialShort bench or jury trialJury trial over days or weeks; investigators and experts

Example (illustrative, not a quote): a misdemeanor resolved in 10 hours at the $216 Clio criminal average: 10 × $216 = $2,160. A felony that takes 60 hours through a plea: 60 × $216 = $12,960. The same 60 hours at the $349 all-lawyer average: 60 × $349 = $20,940. Trial can multiply the hours.

Bail is not a legal fee

Families often confuse bail with the lawyer's fee. They are separate:

  • Cash bail paid to the court is generally returned at the end of the case if the defendant makes every court date, though some courts deduct fines or costs first.
  • A bail bond premium paid to a bail bond company is the company's fee and is not returned. Some states restrict or do not use commercial bail.
  • The lawyer's fee is a separate contract. Do not assume posted bail can later be used to pay the lawyer; ask the court and the lawyer before relying on it.

Money used for bail is money you cannot use for a lawyer. If funds are limited, talk to a lawyer before posting a large bond, because a lawyer can sometimes argue for release on lower bail or on conditions.

When a relative pays

A parent or partner can pay the fee, but the lawyer represents the defendant, not the payer. California's Rule 1.8.6, for example, permits third-party payment only if it does not interfere with the lawyer's independent judgment, the client's information remains confidential, and the client gives informed written consent [8]. The payer should not expect to direct the defense or receive details of the case.

Questions to ask before you hire

  • Is the fee flat or hourly? Exactly which stages does it cover, and what is the trial fee?
  • Are investigators, experts or transcripts extra?
  • Is any part non-refundable, and what is refunded if the case is dismissed early?
  • How many cases like mine have you handled in this courthouse?
  • Do you offer payment plans?

For specific charges, see DUI lawyer cost, drug trafficking lawyer cost, white-collar crime lawyer cost and federal criminal defense lawyer cost. Your state page lists the bar's lawyer referral service.

faq.q: Do I qualify for a public defender?
faq.a: It depends on your state's test, which looks at income, assets and household size. Florida, for example, treats income at or below 200% of the federal poverty guidelines as indigent. Ask for appointed counsel at your first appearance and be ready to fill out a financial form.

faq.q: Why do criminal lawyers ask for the whole fee up front?
faq.a: Because they cannot take a share of any outcome and much of the work happens early. Fees paid in advance must be held in trust and earned as work is done; ask what is refunded if the case ends early.

faq.q: Can I use my bail money to pay my lawyer?
faq.a: Not automatically. Cash bail is held by the court and returned after the case if all court dates are met, sometimes minus fines or costs. A bail bond premium is never returned. Ask the court and your lawyer before counting on bail funds.

faq.q: Is a misdemeanor lawyer worth it if I plan to plead guilty?
faq.a: Often, because a lawyer can check the evidence, negotiate a lesser charge or diversion, and explain consequences for your license, job or immigration status before you plead. If jail is possible and you cannot pay, ask for appointed counsel.
